info.bio:
Soundgarden fue una banda de rock estadounidense formada en Seattle, Washington en 1984. Integrada por Chris Cornell en la guitarra y voz, Kim Thayil como guitarra principal, Matt Cameron en la bateria y Ben Shepherd en el bajo, tras abandonar Hiro Yamamoto el grupo después de grabar el disco Louder Than Love.
Cornell se mantuvo en la banda hasta su muerte en Mayo de 2017.

Se les suele considerar como una de las cuatro grandes bandas del grunge junto a Nirvana, Alice in Chains y Pearl Jam.

Green River lo inauguran (Come On Down) y Pearl Jam, Soundgarden, Melvins y Mudhoney fijan sus cuatro puntos cardinales; Nirvana, con Nevermind, lo convierten en una tragaperras y en la banda sonora de la crisis nerviosa de una generación. Después, Alice In Chains (Dirt), Foo Fighters, Hammerbox, GodHeadSilo, Everclear, Stone Temple Pilots, Tool (el grupo más innovador de la segunda generación: Aenima, Lateralus), God Machine, Helmet, Quicksand, Urge Overkill, los Smashing Pumpkins (Siamese Dream, Mellon Collie), Scarce, Creed, Bush, Manic Street Preachers, Silverchair.

podcast.title: Formation (1984) – Early Lineup Changes
podcast.body: Soundgarden officially started in 1984 with Chris Cornell, Hiro Yamamoto, and Kim Thayil, and an initial drummer Scott Sunquist. Sunquist was later replaced by Matt Cameron due to family commitments involving a wife and child. "In 1984, they started calling themselves Soundgarden with a German name Scott Sunquist. But he had a wife and child and couldn't commit to the band full time, so he was replaced by Matt Cameron."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Deep Six Compilation (1985) – First Soundgarden Recordings
podcast.body: The original 1984 lineup of Soundgarden (Cornell, Yamamoto, Sundquist on drums, and Kim Thayil on guitar) recorded their first material in 1985. Three tracks appeared on a compilation called *Deep Six* issued by Seattle's CZ Records, including a track called "Here We Tick." "That would be the original lineup of Soundgarden from 1984."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Management by Susan Silver (1985-1998)
podcast.body: Susan Silver started managing Soundgarden in 1985, formalizing the arrangement by 1986. Her initial motivation was a "starry-eyed idea of helping bands reach their dreams." Silver continued to manage the band until 1998, a year after their 1997 breakup, at which point she shut down her company, Silver Management.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hiro Yamamoto's Departure (1989) – Pursuit of Education
podcast.body: In 1989, bassist Hiro Yamamoto left Soundgarden to finish his master's degree in physical chemistry. After leaving the band, he continued his musical pursuits by playing in a band called Truly, which included members of Screaming Trees. "In 1989, there was a lineup change when bass player Hero Yamamoto quit to finish his master's degree in physical chemistry."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Marriage to Chris Cornell (1990)
podcast.body: Susan Silver began dating Soundgarden's singer, Chris Cornell, about a year before she formally managed the band. They married in 1990 and, initially, their personal and professional lives were successfully kept separate, with many Soundgarden fans unaware that the singer was married to the manager.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Grunge Scene Status (1991)
podcast.body: In early 1991, during the filming of *Singles*, Soundgarden had signed to a major label and released their *Louder Than Love* album, but their music had not yet gained significant recognition outside the metal community. This illustrates that the Seattle grunge scene was largely unknown to the wider public at that time, predating its explosion into mainstream culture. "Yes, Soundgarden had signed to a major label and had released their louder than love album, but outside the metal community, it didn't really register."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Cameo in Singles (1992)
podcast.body: Soundgarden made a cameo appearance in the 1992 Hollywood motion picture *Singles*. The film not only featured the music of the moment but also included appearances from key figures and bands of the burgeoning alternative and grunge scene, contributing to its growing visibility. "It was a Hollywood motion picture that not only featured the music of the moment, but also cameos from Pearl Jam and Chris Cornell and Allison Chains."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Grammy Nomination (1992)
podcast.body: Soundgarden was nominated for a Grammy in 1992, which they ultimately lost to R.E.M. "they ended up being nominated for a Grammy in 1992, which they lost to the aforementioned REM."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lollapalooza 1992 Main Stage Act
podcast.body: Soundgarden was among the major bands performing on the main stage of the 1992 Lollapalooza Festival, a lineup described as one of the best in the event's history. "Sound garden, Pearl Jam, ministry, ice cube. That was just the main stage."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Popularity in Late 1992
podcast.body: By late summer 1992, Soundgarden had achieved widespread popularity, driving the success of a 1991 side project, Temple of the Dog. This collaborative tribute album to Andrew Wood broke into the album chart's top 10 and belatedly went platinum. "By the late summer of 92, both Pearl Jam and Soundgarden were so popular with new fans hungry for new material that a tiny side project they'd collaborated on back in 1991 called Temple of the Dog."

podcast.title: Regurgitation Cocktail Drinking Contest (1992)
podcast.body: During the 1992 Lollapalooza tour, Chris Cornell participated in a drinking contest with Eddie Vedder, where they consumed a cocktail of goo, bile, and half-digested food regurgitated by Matt "The Tube" Crowley. Chris Cornell lost this contest to Eddie Vedder. "Eddie Vetter and Chris Cornell decided they would have a drinking contest. And the drink was the stuff pumped out of Matt the tube crowley's stomach."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Wayne's World Soundtrack Contribution (1992)
podcast.body: Soundgarden was featured on the first *Wayne's World* soundtrack, released in 1992. While the album was primarily composed of classic rock, it notably included tracks from contemporary alternative bands like Soundgarden and Red Hot Chili Peppers. "However, it does feature the chili peppers and soundcard."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Breakup (April 9, 1997) – Official Announcement
podcast.body: Soundgarden officially broke up on April 9, 1997. This event made Chris Cornell a free agent, allowing him to pursue a solo career and other projects, including Audioslave. "Soundgarden broke up on April 9th, 1997 with an official announcement, making Chris a free agent."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Sudden Breakup (1997)
podcast.body: Soundgarden unexpectedly announced their disbandment on April 9, 1997, stunning fans. The band was known as one of the best and biggest acts of the Grunge era. "When Soundgarden decided to call it a day with a sudden announcement on April 9th of 1997, fans were kind of stunned."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Divorce Litigation (2003)
podcast.body: After Chris Cornell and Susan Silver divorced in 2003, a lawsuit ensued. Chris sued for $1 million in damages, alleging that Silver, as Soundgarden's manager, diverted money owed to him to other band members. The suit also claimed she withheld his guitars, demos, journals, notes, and two Grammy Awards statues, and sought to permanently bar her from representing Soundgarden due to "irreconcilable conflicts of interest," which explained the delay in a Soundgarden reunion.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Reunion and Subsequent End (2010-2017)
podcast.body: Soundgarden, despite a "bad breakup" in 1997, put their differences aside in 2010 to reunite, record, and perform. Their reunion, part of a wider trend driven by declining CD sales and promoters' need for established acts, lasted until Chris Cornell's death in 2017. "Boomgarten, a band that had a bad breakup in 1997, put all their differences aside in 2010 and continued to record and perform until Chris Cornell died in 2017."

podcast.title: Final Performance with Chris Cornell (May 17, 2017)
podcast.body: Soundgarden played a show at the Fox Theatre in Detroit on May 17, 2017. This performance would be Chris Cornell's last, and it elicited mixed reactions, with some observers noting that "something was off" with Cornell, while others felt the band was performing strongly. "On May 17, 2017, Soundgarden played a show at the Fox Theatre in Detroit. Depending on who you ask, the band was either on fire or that something was off."

podcast.title: Appearance on Deep Six
podcast.body: Soundgarden was one of the groups that appeared on the "Deep Six" compilation, which showcased the burgeoning Seattle music scene. "Other groups to appear on the Deep Six compilation included a new band called Soundgarden, a band called Green River featuring guitarist Jeff Amit, who would later go on to a former group called Pearl Jam."

podcast.title: Backmasking in Digital Era
podcast.body: Soundgarden is mentioned as an artist using backward messages, particularly in the post-CD era where digital sound editing tools facilitated the technique's return. "Back, cake, cold play, M&M, Fransford Nand, Lincoln Park, Marilyn Manson, Moby Soundgarden Tool, 21 Pilots, and a ton more."

podcast.title: Ben Shepherd's Bass Playing Style
podcast.body: Bassist Ben Shepherd was noted for his distinctive playing, often using power chords on his bass, which contributed to Soundgarden's heavy sound. "Ben Shepherd of SoundGarden practically played power chords on his bass sometime."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ben Shepherd's Enduring Role – Roadie to Bassist
podcast.body: Ben Shepherd eventually replaced Jason Everman as Soundgarden's bassist and has held the position since. Before joining Soundgarden, Shepherd was active in the Seattle scene, playing in bands like March of Crimes (briefly with Stone Gossard) and Tick Dolly Roe (with Chad Channing), and even freelanced as Nirvana's roadie before being briefly considered for their second guitarist role. "But that was still okay because he auditioned for Soundgarden again and got the job, and he still has that job today."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Black Calivados – Chris Cornell's Parisian Restaurant
podcast.body: Chris Cornell invested in and owned a restaurant in Paris named Black Calivados, which he opened around the time he fell in love with publicist Vicki Cariannis, daughter of a New York restaurant executive. The restaurant is described as "very hip, very expensive," with decor designed by the individual responsible for Victoria's Secret fashion shows. The menu offers "New American" cuisine, featuring dishes like Caramelized Quail, Truffled Mac and Cheese, and Peanut Butter, Soul, and Popcorn Fois Gras, with a burger priced at approximately 40 euros. "But modeling is a fickle thing, so Chris decided to sink money into a restaurant in Paris called Black Calivados."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: British Reception
podcast.body: In 1990, British listeners showed greater initial enthusiasm for the Seattle sound than Americans, with two Soundgarden singles making the lower rungs of the UK chart. "At first, British listeners were more enamored of the Seattle sound than Americans were."

podcast.title: Chris Cornell's Availability Post-Soundgarden
podcast.body: After the dissolution of Soundgarden, Chris Cornell had not been actively involved in many projects. This made him available when producer Rick Rubin connected him with the instrumental members of Rage Against the Machine, leading to their collaboration and the formation of Audioslave. "Now Chris hadn't been doing very much since the dissolution of Soundgarden, so why not see if there was any chemistry there?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Chris Cornell's Modeling for John Varvatos
podcast.body: Chris Cornell, formerly of Audioslave and Soundgarden, engaged in modeling for fashion designer John Varvatos in 2006. This venture was a temporary pursuit, as modeling is described as a "fickle thing." "A guy who did modeling for Vavardos in 2006 was Chris Cornell, ex of audio-slave and sound-garden."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Chris Cornell's Pre-Music Career in Seafood and Culinary Arts
podcast.body: Before his musical career, Chris Cornell worked as a fish cutter for a seafood wholesaler in Seattle, where his responsibilities included gutting fish. He eventually advanced his culinary skills to become a sous chef at Ray's Boat House, a restaurant also located in Seattle. "Back before the whole music thing happened, he worked cutting up fish for a seafood wholesaler in Seattle."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Chris Cornell's Prior Band
podcast.body: Chris Cornell, who became the singer for Audioslave, was formerly associated with Soundgarden. "Chris Cornell of Soundguard doing the singing."

podcast.body: The Hypnosis Song Fund acquired Chris Cornell's shares in all Soundgarden songs and all his solo material. "The Hypnosis song fun owns the share of the song once held by Chris Cornell. In fact, Hypnosis owns all of Chris's former shares in all Sound Garden songs and all his solo material too."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Chris Cornell's Solo Struggles
podcast.body: In 2001, producer Rick Rubin noted that Soundgarden was not getting back together and Chris Cornell's solo work had not gained traction, prompting him to suggest Cornell join forces with the instrumental members of Rage Against the Machine. "Chris Cardell's solo work is okay, but it hasn't gained him any traction."

podcast.title: Deep Six Contribution
podcast.body: Soundgarden was among the local bands that contributed songs to the pivotal "Deep Six" compilation in the fall of 1985, an early effort to document the emerging musical identity of the Pacific Northwest. "Other groups to appear on the Deep Six compilation included a new band called Soundgarden."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Defection to Major Label
podcast.body: Soundgarden was one of the "bigger bands" in the Seattle scene that major record labels successfully recruited, eventually defecting from Subpop to sign with a major label. "Major record labels had heard about the developing scene and they were in town, snapping up some of the bigger bands. ...Soundgarden defected to a major."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early 90s Grunge Influence
podcast.body: Soundgarden was a significant act in the grunge movement that began in late 1991, and their music was enthusiastically absorbed by teenagers during their coming-of-age years.

podcast.title: Early Formation and Grunge Candidate Status
podcast.body: Soundgarden was founded in 1984 and began performing in 1985, placing its origins in the mid-80s, earlier than Nirvana's first album. The band is considered a strong candidate for marking one of the significant inflection points that started grunge music. "son guarden se fundan en el 84, ya concieron los 85, entonces posicionaría la música grancha bastante anterior al primer disco en Irvana."

podcast.title: Early Mainstream Breakthrough
podcast.body: Their 1989 album "Louder Than Love" was the first Grunge LP to chart on Billboard, reaching number 108 in early 1990. Despite this, the Seattle scene had not yet become a mainstream phenomenon, and Grunge was not a recognized term in the music press, with the band still marketed as metal. "Louder Than Love, became the first Grunge LP to make the Billboard album chart, where it reached number 108 in early 1990."

podcast.title: Early Subpop Roster
podcast.body: By mid-1988, Soundgarden was a notable local group featured on the roster of Subpop, which was considered a "pretty cool little label" at the time. "The roster featured local groups like Soundgarden, Screaming Trees and Mud Honey."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Evolving Sound
podcast.body: In the mid-1990s, Soundgarden was noted for evolving its sound into something distinct from its initial grunge identity. This development reflected a broader trend among pioneering grunge bands to explore new musical directions. "Soundgarten was evolving into something different."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First Grunge Band to Sign Major Label Deal
podcast.body: Soundgarden was the first grunge band to secure a major label record deal. This signing marked an early step for the grunge genre into mainstream music industry recognition. "They were also the first grunge band to sign a major label record deal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Ongoing History Book of Firsts

podcast.title: Formation and Early Lineup
podcast.body: Soundgarden was formed in 1984, taking its name from a local Seattle sculpture. The band originated with Chris Cornell (vocals, drums) and Hiro Yamamoto (bass). Kim Thayil joined on guitar, and Matt Cameron became the permanent drummer in 1986 after Cornell transitioned solely to vocals. Yamamoto later left in the late 80s, with Ben Shepherd eventually taking over bass duties. "Soundgarden formed in 1984. They named themselves after a local Seattle sculpture."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Genre Definition
podcast.body: Soundgarden played a significant role in refining the Grunge template, notably fusing punk and new wave elements with hard rock and metal. Guitarist Kim Thayil characterized their 1988 album "Ultramega OK" as "Sabbath-influenced punk." "What made Grunge a term by the way that none of the bands tagged as Grunge either liked or adopted was how it fused punk and new wave into hard rock and even metal."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Global Alt Rock Explosion
podcast.body: Soundgarden was among the groups whose sounds propelled the alt rock attitude into a worldwide phenomenon in the 1990s, reinforcing the guitar-centric nature of alt rock during that decade. "thanks to groups like Nirvana and Pearl Jam and Sound Guard and Allison Chained and smashing pumpkins and stone-tiple pile with and so on."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Grunge Invasion Threat
podcast.body: Soundgarden was explicitly named as one of the "grunge marauders" from the US whose music threatened to "swamp" the UK scene and against whom British rock traditions needed to be saved. "It all needed to be saved from the likes of Nirvana and Pearl Jam and Soundgarden."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Grunge Invasion of UK (Early 1990s)
podcast.body: Soundgarden was one of the American bands associated with the grunge movement that invaded the UK in the early 1990s, contributing to the supplanting of traditional British rock and inspiring a defensive reaction from British musicians. "For a while, the proud tradition of British rock and wool was being supplanted by bands like Pearl Jam and Nirvana and Soundgarden."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: Grunge Movement Leader
podcast.body: Soundgarden was a key band in the grunge movement, contributing "riff-ready songs" that caused alt-rock to coalesce around hard guitar rock. They were instrumental in the genre's rise to mainstream prominence.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Grunge Trilogy
podcast.body: Soundgarden is identified as one of the three major bands forming the "Grunge trilogy" that officially began between 1981 and 1991 in the United States. "venía la gran trilogía del gruncho, aparecía Nirvana, aparecía Soundgarden, aparecía Pell Jam."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Influence of Grunge on Rock
podcast.body: Soundgarden was instrumental in bridging the "attitude gap" between rock and old-school metal throughout the early and mid-90s. Along with Nirvana and Alice in Chains, they openly cited bands like Black Sabbath, Judas Priest, and Kiss as "huge influences" on their music, contributing to a new open-mindedness in the rock scene. "Boys like Kurt Cobain and the dudes from Soundguard, Dinales and Chains weren't shy about saying, hey, don't diss black Sabbath and Judas Priest and kiss, they were pretty good bands."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Jason Everman's Brief Stint – Nirvana Connection
podcast.body: Jason Everman replaced Hiro Yamamoto on bass but did not remain with Soundgarden for long. He was notable for his prior involvement with Nirvana, where he briefly served as second guitarist, toured behind their *Bleach* album, and even paid the $606.17 recording fee for that album, receiving fake credit for his financial generosity. "Jason didn't last very long in Soundgarden either and was eventually replaced by Ben Shepard."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Legal Fight Post-Chris Cornell's Death
podcast.body: Following Chris Cornell's death in May 2017, the remaining members of Soundgarden entered into a prolonged legal dispute over the future of the band with Cornell's widow, Vicki Cornell. The band had been back together, recording and touring, seemingly settled into a new phase of their career before the tragedy. "And there's been a legal fight over the future of Soundgarden ever since."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lollapalooza Performance with Ramones
podcast.body: Soundgarden performed alongside the Ramones and Metallica on the Lollapalooza tour in 1996, which was part of the Ramones' extended farewell. "Part of the long farewell even included some dates on the Lala Paloza tour that year, performing alongside Metallica and Soundgarden."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Ongoing History Book of Lasts

podcast.title: Long Road to Attention
podcast.body: Soundgarden had been working to gain attention since 1984, finally breaking through with "Badmotorfinger" in 1991, following the success of Nirvana and Pearl Jam. "Soundgarten had been laboring to get some kind of attention since 1984"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lyrical Comparisons
podcast.body: The lyrics of Melvins' 1987 album *Gluey Porch Treatments* are noted for their resemblance to Soundgarden's lyrics, as well as those of Nirvana and Pearl Jam. "no recordan algunas letras de Soundgarden."

podcast.title: Major Label Reputation Building
podcast.body: By the time the Temple of the Dog album was released, Soundgarden was actively building their reputation, having already secured a new major label record deal. "Soundgarden was well into building their reputation with a new major label record deal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Metaphorical Lyrical Approach
podcast.body: Soundgarden was cited as an example of a Grunge band whose lyrics often employed metaphors, a stylistic choice that differentiated them from the more literal, "first person approach" adopted by Post-Grunge lyricists. "Compare how many songs by Nirvana Pro Jam, Alice and Change and Soundgarden used the word I in the lyrics."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Music Reflecting Electric Guitar's Origin
podcast.body: Soundgarden's music is presented as an example of a song based on the electric guitar. The existence of the electric guitar was made possible by the inheritances of several individuals over a century ago, linking diverse historical factors to modern rock music. "Soundgarten, with a song based on the electric guitar, which was made possible by the inheritances of a couple of people more than a hundred years ago."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Opened for Guns N' Roses
podcast.body: Soundgarden was chosen to open for Guns N' Roses on their "Use Your Illusion" tour, an opportunity that Nirvana declined. "They were picked to open for guns and roses on the Usur illusion tour"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Grunge Evolution and Reunion
podcast.body: Soundgarden sold millions of records during the height of grunge and later reunited, playing to sold-out arenas. Their journey eventually saw the tragic death of Chris Cornell, and the band subsequently broke up. "Sound Garden reunited and played to solo de Rinas and then Chris Cornell died."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Predecessor to Audioslave
podcast.body: Soundgarden is identified as one of the two "previous incarnations" that Audioslave embodied. The flame sculpture on Audioslave's debut album cover explicitly symbolizes "the memory of two previous incarnations, namely Soundgarden and Rage Against the Machine." "The flame is the eternal flame, or the flame of remembrance, embodying the memory of two previous incarnations, namely Soundgarden and Rage Against the Machine."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Stories Behind Iconic Album Covers Part 2

podcast.title: Reunion Delay – Linked to Lawsuit
podcast.body: The legal dispute between Chris Cornell and his ex-wife and former manager, Susan Silver, regarding alleged diverted royalties and withheld band property, contributed to the delay in Soundgarden's reunion. This conflict involved claims of fraud, oppression, and malice. "So if you've ever wondered why it took so long for the Soundgarden reunion to come together, there's part of your answer."

xref.title: Death (May 17–18, 2017) – MGM Grand Detroit, Ativan, Unknown Barbiturates, Naloxone Found in System
xref.body: After a Soundgarden show at the MGM Grand in Detroit, Cornell returned to room 1136. His wife Vicki, 2,000 miles away in Los Angeles, noticed the house lights flickering via a remote app on Chris's phone and called him at 11:35pm — twenty minutes after he left the stage. His bodyguard Martin had given him two Ativan (lorazepam) tablets beforehand to help him sleep. Cornell told Vicki he was fine but sounded groggy and slurred. Martin was sent to check on him at 12:15am, found the room locked, kicked the door in, found the bathroom locked, kicked that door in, and found Chris on the floor with blood from his mouth and an exercise band around his neck. A hotel medic arrived at 12:56am; paramedics followed; Chris was pronounced dead at 1:30am. The official cause was suicide by hanging. Toxicology found Ativan, unknown barbiturates, and unexplained Nalozone (naloxone, an anti-opioid) in his system. A hidden injury was mentioned in two clinical reports but not in the autopsy. In 2018 Vicki sued Dr. Robert Coblin of Beverly Hills, who had prescribed the Ativan, alleging dangerous over-prescription to a known former addict; the lawsuit settled out of court in May 2021. "Many of us who know Chris well noticed that he wasn't himself during his final hours and that something was very off."

xref.title: Death by Suicide (May 18, 2017)
xref.body: Chris Cornell died by suicide by hanging on May 18, 2017, at 1:30 AM, a death that came as a "real shock" to many. He was found in his hotel room (room 1136 at the MGM Grand, Detroit) with a red exercise band around his neck, attached to a carabiner jammed tightly into the doorframe. The night before, May 17, Soundgarden played a show at the Fox Theatre in Detroit, after which his long-time tour manager felt Chris was "messed up and struggling." Back at the hotel, his bodyguard, Martin Kirsten, gave him two Ativan pills, for which Chris had a prescription. Shortly after, Chris spoke to his wife Vicki, who noted his slurred speech; he claimed to have taken "too much Ativan" and was "just tired." He abruptly hung up, alarming Vicki. Martin Kirsten, called by Vicki, found Chris's room latched from the inside. After kicking open both the room and bathroom doors, he found Chris. The toxicology report found Ativan (four doses), pseudoephedrine, butylbital, caffeine, and Narcan (administered by paramedics). While his wife speculated drugs contributed to an "altered mental state," the police ruled it suicide by hanging. "Chris was pronounced dead at 1.30, and the police ruled a suicide by hanging."

xref.title: Jason Everman – Paid for Bleach, Joined Nirvana, Quit, Joined Soundgarden, Quit, Became Special Forces Soldier
xref.body: Jason Everman financed the entire $606.17 recording cost of Nirvana's *Bleach* album as a favor and was falsely credited in the liner notes as having played on it. He later genuinely joined the band as second guitarist in February 1989, made his debut on February 25, 1989, and was dismissed or quit after a final show at the Pyramid Club in New York City on July 18, 1989. He subsequently joined Soundgarden as bassist, appearing on the EP *Loudest Love* (1990) and a world tour before leaving again. He then joined the US Army, served multiple tours in Afghanistan and Iraq as an elite Special Forces soldier comparable to SEAL Team 6, received an honorable discharge in 2006, enrolled in Columbia University to study philosophy, and now lives quietly in rural Washington State. "Two of the biggest grunge bands of all time, and he left both of them."

xref.body: Following their 2004 divorce, Chris Cornell sued Susan Silver for a million dollars, accusing her of diverting Soundgarden royalties to the other band members and withholding valuable items such as a guitar, Grammy Awards, demo tapes, personal recordings, diaries, and journals. The suit used strong terms like "fraud, oppression, and malice" in its documentation, and it was eventually settled. "Chris sued Susan for a million dollars, claiming that she diverted Soundgarden royalties away from him and to the other three band members, words like fraud, oppression, and malice reused in the documents."

xref.title: Lifelong Struggles with Mental Health, Drugs, and Alcohol
xref.body: Cornell grew up as a loner, one of six children raised by a single mother who was an alcoholic; his estranged father was also an alcoholic. By age 12 he was drinking, smoking marijuana, and taking prescription medications. He tried PCP at 14 and suffered a very bad experience, deepening his depression and anxiety. He managed his mental health throughout Soundgarden's existence but after the band broke up in 1997 — coinciding with the failure of his first marriage — he went heavily into heroin and oxycodone. He entered rehab in 2002 and was entirely sober by 2005, except for prescription drugs. "No one really knows what one of the mill depression is. You'll think that someone has run of the mill depression and then the next thing you know, they're hanging from a rope."

xref.title: Origins at Ray's Boathouse – Kitchen Work Led to Singing Career
xref.body: In the early 1980s, long before Soundgarden existed, Cornell worked at a Seattle restaurant called Ray's Boathouse, starting as a teenager when his older brother Peter got him a job. He progressed from dishwasher to busboy to sous chef. At the restaurant's annual staff Christmas party, he spontaneously grabbed the microphone from a hired two-man band and launched into "Twist and Shout," astonishing everyone with the power of his voice. The bass player at Ray's Boathouse was Hiro Yamamoto; a maintenance worker named Scott Sundquist (later replaced by Matt Cameron) completed the original 1984 Soundgarden lineup with Kim Thayil on guitar. "Nobody had heard him before and nobody could believe the power of this kid's voice."

This made them the first Grunge band to record at that studio, which later became famous for hosting bands like Nirvana, Alice in Chains, Soundgarden, The Melvins, and Mudhoney. xref.title: Post-Death Lawsuits – Seven Demo Vocal Tracks, Royalties, Tribute Concert Proceeds
xref.body: After Cornell's death, Vicki Cornell filed suits over two primary issues: the rights to seven vocal demo tracks recorded in early 2017 on his laptop, apparently destined for a new Soundgarden album, and the disbursement of Soundgarden royalties. Soundgarden counter-sued, alleging Vicki misappropriated proceeds from a 2019 tribute concert. Both sides went to war over social media rights and Chris's posthumous participation in any band activities. Vicki's offer of $4 million per remaining member, then $7 million, was refused. A settlement was announced on April 17, 2023: the seven songs will be finished and released. "This dispute has never been about money or the band. This is their life's work and their legacy."

xref.title: Symbolism of "Audioslave" Album Cover
xref.body: Storm Thorgerson, designer of Audioslave's 2002 debut album cover, explained its profound symbolism. The solitary figure in the landscape represents "pilgrims or slaves of sound."
